spike_candidates.statement: In 1904 the public had about 1.4 square inches of Coney Island beachfront per New Yorker, and a 1913 court ruling gave the beach back to the state.
spike_candidates.tension: The famous free people's beach was private, fenced and sold off until courts and a 1921 land taking reopened it.

spike_candidates.statement: Nobody paid at the sand: in the Depression Luna Park admitted it could not compete with a beach that charged no admission.
spike_candidates.tension: The free beach and the five-cent subway, not the rides, were what the poor of New York actually bought.

spike_candidates.statement: On 29 July 1907 Steeplechase burned and George Tilyou posted a sign selling admission to the burning ruins for ten cents.
spike_candidates.tension: The fire cleared 35 acres and the owner turned the disaster into a ticket sale the next morning.

spike_candidates.statement: In 1946 Steeplechase's pool used a pass scheme that locked out African Americans while Black visitors were a growing share of the park.
spike_candidates.tension: The 'everyone's playground' story had a quiet color line, and no source in this bundle documents the beach itself.

spike_candidates.statement: From 1903 to 1943 a doctor who probably was not a doctor kept premature babies alive in a 25-cent Luna Park sideshow.
spike_candidates.tension: Mainstream medicine rejected incubators, so premature infants were saved by an amusement-park ticket window.

conflicts: Coney Island House founding: 1824 (NYC Parks sign, H016) vs 1829 (Wikipedia Coney Island, H015); Riegelmann Boardwalk Wikipedia says only 'early 19th century'. NYC Parks is the official source but Wikipedia is footnoted; treat 1824-1829 as a range and say 'in the 1820s'.

Boardwalk cost: $3 million for beach and boardwalk construction (NYC Parks sign, H068) vs $20 million for boardwalk plus related improvements (Wikipedia, H067). They are different scopes; the sign likely counts only the beach project. Use both with scope stated; NYC Parks is more authoritative on its own project.

Boardwalk flooring: Douglas fir from Washington State (Wikipedia, H069) vs long leaf yellow pine (NYC Parks, H070). NYC Parks is official; Wikipedia may cite the trade press American Lumberman. Unresolved; avoid asserting species or say 'sources differ'.
Boardwalk opening year: 1922 (Steeplechase Park Wikipedia says it opened in 1922) vs 15 May 1923 (RB, NYC Parks, H064, H065). Resolved: first segment October 1922, full opening 15 May 1923.
Boardwalk east end: Brighton 15th Street (Wikipedia) vs Corbin Place (NYC Parks sign); also later extension east to Brighton and the 1941 extension. Eastern end shifted over time.

Manhattan Beach Hotel size: 150 rooms (Wikipedia Coney Island, H024) vs 300 guest rooms with private baths (Heart of Coney Island, H023). Neither is authoritative; avoid a number or give 'between 150 and 300 by differing accounts'.
Manhattan Beach hotel opening: July 1877 with President Grant presiding (H022) vs 4 July 1877 'immense crowd' (Heart of Coney Island). Compatible only if both are early July 1877.

Elephantine Colossus height and stories: 122 ft, seven stories (Wikipedia, H087) vs twelve stories (Brooklyn Public Library, H088; 6sqft says 12 stories, 150 feet; NYT 1885 headline in Wikipedia references says 'nearly two hundred feet'). Wikipedia's article is flagged for citation problems; treat height as disputed.

Couney's Luna Park run: 1903-1943 (CIHP, H120; History.com says from 1903) vs 1904-1943 (ASU, H121). Luna Park opened May 1903, so 1903 is possible; CIHP is the local museum and more specific. Dreamland exhibit 1904-1911.

Couney casualty figures: more than 8,000 treated, over 6,500 lived (ASU, H118); CIHP says by 1939 treated more than 8,000 and saved 6,500; History.com says Couney claimed an 85 percent success rate and 6,500 saved. These are Couney's own claims; 6,500/8,000 is about 81 percent, not 85.

Luna Park end date: shut by fire 13 Aug 1944, eastern half closed Sept 1944 (Luna Wikipedia, H103) vs closed 1946 (Steeplechase Wikipedia) vs Couney exhibit ending 1943 (ASU). Rides on Surf Avenue operated into 1945. Safe statement: destroyed by fire in 1944, never reopened as a full park.
Luna Park area: 22 acres at 1903 opening vs 38 acres from 1904 expansion vs 50 acres by 1926 (Luna Wikipedia). Not a conflict; different years.
Steeplechase tilyou beach: Steeplechase Wikipedia says a judge in 1913 and appellate in 1916 (H053, H054); Riegelmann Wikipedia says the same, with the 1912 lawsuit (H055).

Creek infill dates: 1920s-30s (Coney Island Wikipedia, H148), by 1924 and Belt Parkway 1930s and 1962 (Creek Wikipedia, H143-H145), early 20th century (HDC). The creek was filled in stages; do not say the island 'became a peninsula in 1962' alone.

Subway fare: 5 cents from 1904 to 1948 (Popik citing Wikipedia, H137) vs Atlas Obscura claim that fare dropped from ten to five cents in 1920 (H138). The 1920 date refers to the BMT line reaching Coney Island at a single five-cent fare (H062); the ten-cent figure is probably the earlier surface-rail plus subway or train combination. Atlas Obscura's claim is the weakest.

Hot dog origin: Feltman 1867 pie wagon and later bun hot dog (6sqft, H126) vs Heart of Coney Island 'charles feltman invented the hot dog'. Both are weak (blogs); Barry Popik / WordOrigins show the term 'coney island' for a sausage appears in print by 1895 (H009). Unresolved.

Corbin 'American Society for the Suppression of Jews' (MW Wikipedia) is an extraordinary claim with no support in other bundle sources; do not use. Corbin's interview of 21 July 1879 (H029) and the ban (H031) are supported.
NYC Parks sign says 'as coney island became an important amusement center in the early 19th century'; it is clearly the late 19th century. Treat that sentence as an error (CP source).
dead_ends: No source here documents Lenape presence on the island beyond a 1654 deed and the Techkonis map entry (WordOrigins); nothing from NYC Parks, the Lenape Center or archaeology.

No authoritative source on segregation, race or discrimination on the public beach or boardwalk in 1900-1945 (only the 1946 Steeplechase pool pass and a WWII Coast Guard photo caption). Needs Kasson, BPL or newspaper archives.
No beach-specific content on lifeguards, bathing costume rules, bathhouse prices, beach attendance counts by year, or 1920s-30s beach life; Prohibition-era Coney Island is absent.
No Dreamland source page (opening 1904, tower, Hellgate, founder William Reynolds beyond mentions) in this bundle; Dreamland fire date (May 1911) not given with a day.
The LPC designation report (LP-2583) that scouting flagged was not in the bundle; no official source for beach-creation history beyond the NYC Parks sign and Wikipedia.
No primary sources: Brooklyn Eagle or NYT 1879 Corbin interview, 1894 McKane trial, 1913 court decision, 1921-23 boardwalk records.
Weegee's exact date (21 vs 22 July 1940) is not in these sources; V&A and Whitney give only 1940. No source supports July 4.
Price of a bathing suit, locker or bathhouse rental on the public beach after 1923; cost of subway/train from Manhattan in pre-1920 era beyond the 35-cent Culver fare.
Hot dog invention dispute (1867 vs c.1870) is told only by blogs; no primary evidence.
Population and attendance numbers other than anecdotal ('up to one million' on hot days, 'several million per year').

recency.newest_item: Wikipedia pages in the bundle show 2026 edit dates (Manhattan Beach 24 Sep 2026; Elephantine Colossus 10 Sep 2026). History content is settled; the newest rule-type content (NYC Parks boardwalk material counts, Parks page lists council member Kayla Santosuosso) is undated. No time-sensitive hours, prices or rules are included in this history topic.

facts.fact: The westernmost sand spit was labeled Conyne Eylandt on Dutch maps starting with the 1639 Manatus map.
facts.quote: named conyne eylandt in early-17th-century dutch maps, starting with the 1639 manatus map

facts.fact: Wikipedia says the Lenape called the area Narrioch, possibly meaning land without shadows; WordOrigins calls that translation spurious.
facts.quote: called this area narrioch, possibly meaning "land without shadows

facts.fact: WordOrigins.org says the translation of Narriockh as land of light or no shadow appears to be spurious.
facts.quote: but this translation appears to be spurious

facts.fact: A 1654 Gravesend deed records the Lenape word narriockh as meaning simply the island, and gives the neck of land as manahanung.
facts.quote: called by them narriockh, that is to say, the island

facts.fact: The English name Conyne Island appears in a deed dated 7 May 1654 that conveyed the island from the Lenape to Gravesend settlers.
facts.quote: the name conyne island appears as early as 7 may 1654 in a deed

facts.fact: The Manatus map also marks a Munsee village named Techkonis, which may be the source of the -konis element; nothing else is known of it.
facts.quote: that map also marks a munsee village named techkonis

facts.fact: No origin theory for the name Coney Island has strong evidence, though the Dutch word for rabbit is the most popular.
facts.quote: there is little evidence for each origin theory

facts.fact: Henry Hudson's crewman John Colman did die on Coney Island in 1609, but nothing links him to the name.
facts.quote: colman did indeed die on coney island, but nothing connects him with the name

facts.fact: The phrase Coney Island for a hot dog is recorded by at least 1895, in the Syracuse Daily Standard of 6 September.
facts.quote: this appellation goes back to at least 1895

facts.fact: The 1645 purchase of southern Brooklyn from the Native Americans was later said to be a gun, a blanket and a kettle.
facts.quote: the goods were not recorded in the deed, but later accounts mention a gun, a blanket, and a kettle

facts.fact: Giovanni da Verrazzano is credited as the first European to sight the island, in 1527 and 1529.
facts.quote: giovanni da verrazzano was the first european explorer to sight the island of narrioch during his expeditions to the area in 1527 and 1529

facts.fact: A 1679-80 Dutch journal said nobody lived on the island and it was used in winter to keep livestock.
facts.quote: nobody lives upon it, but it is used in winter for keeping cattle, horses, oxen, hogs and others.

facts.fact: The Jamaica Ditch dug in 1750 cut through Coney Hook and turned the area into separate islands; it is the origin of Coney Island Creek.
facts.quote: was dug through coney hook from brown's creek in the west to hubbard's creek in the east

facts.fact: In 1824 a company built the first bridge across the Jamaica Ditch (now Coney Island Creek), linking the island to the mainland.
facts.quote: built the first bridge across jamaica ditch

facts.fact: The Coney Island House, the island's first hotel, is dated 1829 by Wikipedia.
facts.quote: in 1829, the company also built the first hotel on the island: the coney island house

facts.fact: NYC Parks' historical sign dates the founding of the Coney Island House as a seaside resort to 1824.
facts.quote: in 1824 the coney island house was established as a seaside resort
facts.source_title: Coney Island Beach & Boardwalk highlights - NYC Parks historical sign

facts.fact: Carriage roads and steamships in the 1830s-40s cut the trip to the island from half a day to two hours.
facts.quote: reduced travel time from a formerly half-day journey to two hours

facts.fact: The middle class began coming in 1847 after a ferry line to Norton's Point started.
facts.quote: in 1847, the middle class started going to coney island upon the introduction of a ferry line

facts.fact: The Brooklyn, Bath and Coney Island Railroad was the first railroad to reach Coney Island, opening in 1864.
facts.quote: became the first railroad to reach coney island when it opened in 1864

facts.fact: In the 1870s a 35-cent train ride on the Culver line ran to Surf Avenue, across from a 300-foot iron tower bought from the 1876 Philadelphia Exposition.
facts.quote: for 35 cents, one could ride the prospect park & coney island railroad to the culver depot terminal at surf avenue

facts.fact: Engeman's Brighton Beach hotel could house 5,000 guests a night and feed 20,000 a day.
facts.quote: with rooms for up to 5,000 people nightly and meals for up to 20,000 people daily

facts.fact: Manhattan Beach Hotel opened July 1877 at a ceremony presided over by President Grant.
facts.quote: was opened for business in july 1877 at a ceremony presided over by president ulysses s. grant

facts.fact: A local history site says the Manhattan Beach Hotel had 300 guest rooms with private baths and an elevator.
facts.quote: had 300 guest rooms, all with private baths
facts.source_title: The rise and fall of Corbin's Manhattan Beach resort - Heart of Coney Island

facts.fact: Wikipedia says the Manhattan Beach Hotel had 150 rooms.
facts.quote: the 150-room manhattan beach hotel

facts.fact: The Manhattan Beach bathing pavilion had 12,000 rental bathing suits.
facts.quote: there were 12,000 bathing suits available for rental
facts.source_title: The rise and fall of Corbin's Manhattan Beach resort - Heart of Coney Island

facts.fact: Bathers at Manhattan Beach had electric lights over the beach for evening swims, and lifeguards in catamarans.
facts.quote: for those desiring to bathe in the evening, there were electric lights illuminating the beach
facts.source_title: The rise and fall of Corbin's Manhattan Beach resort - Heart of Coney Island

facts.fact: Manhattan Beach sold balloon rides at five dollars each to a quarter mile up on a cable.
facts.quote: for five dollars each, to a height of a quarter of a mile
facts.source_title: The rise and fall of Corbin's Manhattan Beach resort - Heart of Coney Island

facts.fact: Manhattan Beach hotels held daily concerts and nightly fireworks that drew tens of thousands.
facts.quote: hosted elaborate nightly fireworks displays, drawing tens of thousands of visitors on summer nights

facts.fact: Austin Corbin's famous anti-Jewish interview with the New York Daily Herald took place on 21 July 1879.
facts.quote: on july 21, 1879, he invited a reporter of the new york daily herald to his office
facts.source_title: The rise and fall of Corbin's Manhattan Beach resort - Heart of Coney Island

facts.fact: The press and Christian clergy almost unanimously condemned Corbin's 1879 ban on Jewish guests.
facts.quote: the press and christian clergy were almost unanimous in their condemnation of corbin
facts.source_title: The rise and fall of Corbin's Manhattan Beach resort - Heart of Coney Island

facts.fact: Corbin barred Jewish guests and used restrictive covenants; the policy ended after his death.
facts.quote: austin corbin had restricted jewish guests at his hotel and enacted restrictive covenants

facts.fact: Corbin Place was renamed M. Corbin Place (for Margaret Corbin) in 2007 because of Austin Corbin's antisemitism.
facts.quote: in 2007, it was renamed m. corbin place for american revolutionary war patriot margaret corbin

facts.fact: The town of Gravesend sold about 500 acres of Manhattan Beach shoreline to Corbin for $1,500 in 1876-77, as the local history site tells it.
facts.quote: when corbin was told the amount, $1,500, he sighed and muttered disconsolately
facts.source_title: The rise and fall of Corbin's Manhattan Beach resort - Heart of Coney Island

facts.fact: The $1,500 price worked out to about $3 an acre.
facts.quote: which came to about $3 an acre
facts.source_title: The rise and fall of Corbin's Manhattan Beach resort - Heart of Coney Island

facts.fact: The popular tale that Corbin came to Manhattan Beach to heal a sick son was a convenient rewrite by William Stillwell, says this source.
facts.quote: stillwell was actually re-writing history real-time to suit himself
facts.source_title: The rise and fall of Corbin's Manhattan Beach resort - Heart of Coney Island

facts.fact: Corbin built a 12,000-capacity concrete cycling track at Manhattan Beach in 1895 for $30,000.
facts.quote: in 1895, corbin built a 12,000 capacity third-mile concrete cycling track behind the hotel at a cost of $30,000

facts.fact: The U.S. Coast Guard ran a training station at Manhattan Beach in World War II, with African-American recruits pictured.
facts.quote: the u.s. coast guard operated a training station at manhattan beach during world war ii

facts.fact: John Y. McKane, Gravesend's boss, got a six-year Sing Sing sentence in 1894 for election fraud.
facts.quote: mckane drew a six-year sentence in sing sing
facts.source_title: The rise and fall of John Boss McKane - Heart of Coney Island

facts.fact: In 1893 McKane's machine submitted 2,700 votes when Gravesend had 1,700 registered voters.
facts.quote: mckane had submitted 2,700 votes when gravesend only had 1,700 registered voters
facts.source_title: The rise and fall of John Boss McKane - Heart of Coney Island

facts.fact: McKane told Republican watchers holding a court injunction that injunctions do not go here.
facts.quote: injunctions don't go here!
facts.source_title: The rise and fall of John Boss McKane - Heart of Coney Island

facts.fact: By 1884 McKane's company had built nearly two-thirds of the buildings in Coney Island and Gravesend.
facts.quote: by 1884, mckane's construction company was credited with building nearly two-thirds of all buildings in coney island and gravesend
facts.source_title: The rise and fall of John Boss McKane - Heart of Coney Island

facts.fact: McKane died in 1899, a year after leaving prison.
facts.quote: mckane died several months after a stroke in 1899
facts.source_title: The rise and fall of John Boss McKane - Heart of Coney Island

facts.fact: Sea Lion Park opened in 1895 and was Coney Island's first amusement area to charge admission.
facts.quote: sea lion park opened in 1895 and was coney island's first amusement area to charge entry fees

facts.fact: Tilyou saw the 1893 Chicago Ferris wheel on his honeymoon, then built a half-size one on Surf Avenue.
facts.quote: tilyou built his own half-size version at surf avenue

facts.fact: Steeplechase opened in 1897 as a family park that banned drinking, gambling and prostitution.
facts.quote: drinking was prohibited, as was gambling and prostitution

facts.fact: Steeplechase added a gateway and a new 25-cent admission charge meant to exclude the seedier elements.
facts.quote: along with a new 25-cent admission charge

facts.fact: Steeplechase Park was destroyed by a fire that began in the Cave of the Winds on the early morning of 29 July 1907.
facts.quote: in the early morning of july 29, 1907, a fire started in the cave of the winds attraction

facts.fact: The 1907 fire destroyed about 35 acres of Coney Island.
facts.quote: about 35 acres (14 ha) of coney island was destroyed

facts.fact: The morning after the 1907 fire, Tilyou posted a sign offering admission to the burning ruins for ten cents.
facts.quote: admission to the burning ruins - ten cents

facts.fact: Tilyou paid for rebuilding by selling 100,000 shares and gave a season pass with every $5 stock certificate.
facts.quote: gave a season pass to everyone who bought a $5 stock certificate

facts.fact: The rebuilt Steeplechase centerpiece, the Pavilion of Fun, was a steel-and-glass hall 450 by 280 feet.
facts.quote: a steel-and-glass enclosure measuring 450 by 280 feet

facts.fact: Steeplechase was rebuilt in steel and concrete because the city passed a law restricting combustible wooden structures.
facts.quote: as the municipality had passed a law restricting the construction of combustible wooden structures

facts.fact: A New York court ruled in 1913 that the beach belonged to the state and not to Tilyou and other amusement owners.
facts.quote: a judge ruled in 1913 that the beach actually belonged to the state

facts.fact: An appellate court upheld the 1913 beach ruling in 1916 with an exception for part of Steeplechase Park.
facts.quote: an appellate court affirmed this decision in 1916, with an exception made for part of steeplechase park

facts.fact: In 1912 New York State sued amusement owners for taking private ownership of Coney Island's beach.
facts.quote: new york state sued amusement owners for taking private ownership of coney island's beach

facts.fact: By the mid-19th century the waterfront was split among private owners who put up barriers.
facts.quote: by the mid-19th century, the coney island waterfront was divided among several private entities who erected barriers

facts.fact: In 1904 public beachfront was estimated at 1.4 square inches for each of 3.7 million New Yorkers.
facts.quote: in 1904, it was estimated that there were 1.4 square inches

facts.fact: In 1912 only one street, West 23rd, gave direct public access from Surf Avenue to the beach.
facts.quote: only one street, west 23rd street, had direct public access to the beach from surf avenue

facts.fact: Some stretches of beach were fenced with fences running into the water.
facts.quote: some sections of the beach were enclosed by fences that extended into the water

facts.fact: Borough President Riegelmann said the boardwalk would end poor people standing with faces pressed against wire fences to see the ocean.
facts.quote: poor people will no longer have to stand with their faces pressed against wire fences looking at the ocean

facts.fact: By 1920 overcrowding was common, with up to a million people on the island on the hottest days.
facts.quote: up to one million people filling the island on the hottest days

facts.fact: When the BMT subway reached Coney Island in 1920, the trip became a five-cent ride.
facts.quote: once the bmt subway line reached the area in 1920, the pleasures of coney island were just a five-cent ride away from the steaming city
facts.source_title: Coney Island Beach & Boardwalk highlights - NYC Parks historical sign

facts.fact: City officials broke ground on the boardwalk 1 October 1921, the day the city got title to the beachfront.
facts.quote: city officials held a groundbreaking ceremony on october 1, 1921, the day they obtained title to the land

facts.fact: The boardwalk opened in stages: first section October 1922, extension to West 17th in December 1922, final section 15 May 1923.
facts.quote: the final section of the boardwalk, from west 17th to west 37th street, was officially opened with a ceremony on may 15, 1923

facts.fact: NYC Parks says the boardwalk opened as Coney Island's Fifth Avenue on 15 May 1923.
facts.quote: opened with great fanfare on may 15, 1923
facts.source_title: Coney Island Beach & Boardwalk highlights - NYC Parks historical sign

facts.fact: The beach project needed 1.7 million cubic yards of sand and added 2.5 million square feet of beach.
facts.quote: the immense engineering project required 1.7 million cubic yards of sand to add another 2.5 million square feet to the beach area
facts.source_title: Coney Island Beach & Boardwalk highlights - NYC Parks historical sign

facts.fact: Wikipedia puts the total cost of the boardwalk and related improvements at $20 million.
facts.quote: in total, the boardwalk and related improvement projects cost $20 million

facts.fact: NYC Parks' sign puts the beach improvement and boardwalk at $3 million.
facts.quote: the $3 million beach improvement and boardwalk construction began in 1921
facts.source_title: Coney Island Beach & Boardwalk highlights - NYC Parks historical sign

facts.fact: Wikipedia says the boardwalk was first laid with Douglas fir planks from Washington State.
facts.quote: the boardwalk was first built using douglas fir planks from washington state

facts.fact: NYC Parks says the original flooring was long leaf yellow pine.
facts.quote: including long leaf yellow pine for the flooring
facts.source_title: Coney Island Beach & Boardwalk highlights - NYC Parks historical sign

facts.fact: The boardwalk is 80 feet wide for most of its length and raised 13 or 14 feet above sea level.
facts.quote: the boardwalk is 80 feet (24 m) wide for most of its length

facts.fact: After completion, the Comptroller said it was not a real boardwalk without pergolas and restrooms; the city approved five comfort stations and five pavilions in 1924.
facts.quote: in june 1924, the new york city board of estimate approved the erection of five comfort stations and five beachfront pavilions

facts.fact: Street work for the boardwalk condemned 288 lots, including 175 houses and parts of Steeplechase Park.
facts.quote: entailed condemning 288 lots, including 175 houses and portions of steeplechase park

facts.fact: The finished beach could hold more than half a million people.
facts.quote: the beach could accommodate more than a half-million people when the project was finished

facts.fact: Parks took over the boardwalk in 1938 and Moses said the beaches and boardwalks were never properly planned.
facts.quote: these beaches and boardwalks were never properly planned, and cannot under present conditions be properly maintained and operated

facts.fact: Moses complained the contractor was allowed to dump brown sand instead of good white sand.
facts.quote: the contractor was allowed to deposit brown sand on the beach

facts.fact: Between 1938 and 1941 Parks resurfaced the beach with a 2-foot layer of fine white sand and extended the boardwalk east.
facts.quote: the beach was greatly expanded and entirely resurfaced with a 2-foot layer of fine white sand
facts.source_title: Coney Island Beach & Boardwalk highlights - NYC Parks historical sign

facts.fact: Robert Moses described the beach as so crowded that bathers had less room than in a coffin.
facts.quote: describing the beach as so crowded that bathers had less room than in a coffin
